title: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: W = kL^3; form unchanged during growth \iff k constant

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: then the value of _k_, according to whether it varies or remains constant, will tell us at once whether there has or has not been a tendency to gradual alteration in the general form.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Length and weight in growth”. Scope: fishes and other growing animals of roughly constant density

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: W = kL^3; form unchanged during growth \iff k constant

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-01: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The equation, variables and decision criterion are explicit, and large public fish survey data contain the needed measurements. Direct morphometrics would strengthen attribution specifically to form, but the core relationship is readily testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using repeated or cross-sectional length and weight records, compute k = W/L^3 and test whether it is constant over size or age. Stable k supports geometric similarity at roughly constant density; systematic k changes refute unchanged form or density and can be compared with direct shape data.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Changes in density can alter k without shape change.

Cross-sectional records can confound growth with cohort or sex.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.85
operationalizability: 0.95
analysis feasibility: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The decision variable is the ordinary condition factor, and both a global compilation of length-weight fits and individual survey records are openly downloadable. A small team can test whether k stays constant during growth for many fishes in days. Density and reproductive state confound the step from a changing k to a change of form, and non-fish animals are thinly covered, but the relation as Thompson defined it for fishes is directly testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute k = W/L^3 for individual fish across lengths. A statistically flat k through the growing range would show stable general form at constant density; a systematic trend of k with length would show that form or density is changing while growth continues.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
k mixes shape change with density, gut fullness, and gonad state.

Coverage is far stronger for commercial fishes than for growing animals in general.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.85
analysis feasibility: 0.85
data existence: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.7

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Weight scales as the cube of length (W = k L^3) only while form and density are unchanged, and Thompson expects form to keep changing as long as growth continues; so in real growing fishes k = W / L^3 should NOT be constant across the size range: it should vary systematically with length in most species (in plaice, by his Fig. 21, rising to a maximum near 30 cm and then declining).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The download and derivation are shared with claim ch03-18 (../thompson1917-ch03-18/fetch.py; fetch.py here delegates to it): per species a preliminary OLS of log10 W on log10 L drops 258 fish with |residual| > 0.5 (pre-registered), then fish are binned per species x quarter x 1-cm length class with n, sum and sum of squares of log10 W (derived/ns_ibts_lw_bins.csv). analysis.py keeps taxa with >= 500 fish and a 97.5th/2.5th percentile length ratio >= 3 (20 taxa: 12 teleosts, 5 elasmobranchs, 3 scyphozoan jellyfish), fits log10 W = a + b1 x + b2 x^2 (x = log10 L) by weighted least squares on class means (exact individual-level OLS since all fish in a class share L), tests it against the cube law (b1 = 3, b2 = 0) by F-test, and computes the ratio of fitted k = W/L^3 between its maximum and minimum over the 2.5-97.5 percentile length range; 'variable k' = P < 0.001 and ratio >= 1.10. Within-quarter fits and a fish-only count are reported as sensitivity checks; the plaice k profile by 1-cm class is the pre-registered secondary.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered (claim supported). In ICES NS-IBTS CA records (Q1 and Q3, 2015-2024, individual weights, CANoAtLngt = 1), for every species with at least 500 weighed fish whose 97.5th-percentile length is at least 3 times its 2.5th-percentile length, fit log10 W = a + b1 log10 L + b2 (log10 L)^2 after dropping fish with |residual| > 0.5 log10 units from a preliminary linear fit (pre-registered cleaning). A species has 'variable k' if (i) an F-test rejects the cube law (model with b1 = 3, b2 = 0) at P < 0.001 and (ii) the fitted k = W / L^3 varies by at least 10% (max/min >= 1.10) across the species' 2.5th-97.5th percentile length range. The claim is supported if at least 70% of eligible species have variable k. Secondary, descriptive: in plaice, the 1-cm-bin mean of k is maximal somewhere between 20 and 40 cm and is lower at both smaller and larger lengths.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered (claim refuted). At most 30% of eligible species have variable k (k is effectively constant across the growing range in most fishes, contrary to Thompson's expectation). Between 30% and 70% is 'mixed'. If fewer than 10 species are eligible the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of eligible taxa (14 of 20) in which k = W/L^3 varies by >= 10% across the growing range and the cube law is rejected at P < 0.001

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exactly at the pre-registered 70% threshold; fish only (17 taxa, jellyfish excluded): 11/17 = 0.647; within-quarter fits: 21 of 30 variable

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The first half of the claim (W = k L^3 for an animal of fixed form and density) is geometry and is not tested. The empirical content is Thompson's expectation that k 'is by no means constant' while growth continues, because form keeps changing; the 10% threshold is the amount of k variation that would be clearly visible on his Fig. 21 (plaice k rises about 15% from small fish to the 30-cm maximum). Changes of k can also come from density, gut fullness or gonad state rather than shape (assessors' caveat); the test cannot separate these, so a supporting result shows that k varies, not that form is the reason. Pooling years and quarters mixes seasonal condition cycles into the k-vs-length relation; the analysis therefore also reports results within each quarter as a robustness check (pre-registered, not part of the verdict). Length conversion: LngtCode '1' means LngtClass in cm; '.' or '0' means mm. A single probe request (NS-IBTS 2019 Q1 CA, HTTP status and first record only) was made before this pre-registration to confirm that the web service is reachable.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: ICES DATRAS, North Sea International Bottom Trawl Survey (NS-IBTS): CA (age/weight/maturity) and HH (haul) exchange records, Q1 and Q3, 2015-2024

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The result sits exactly on the pre-registered threshold (14/20 = 70.0%), so the verdict is fragile: excluding the three jellyfish taxa (bell diameter is not a fish length, though they are 'other growing animals' within the claim's scope) gives 11/17 = 65% and the verdict would be 'mixed'. The robust findings are weaker than the verdict label: the cube law is rejected statistically in 19 of 20 taxa (huge samples make any departure significant), the median exponent b is 3.07 (range 2.35-3.38), but only 9 of 20 taxa have |b - 3| > 0.1, and k varies by >= 10% across the central 95% of lengths in 14. So k is 'by no means constant' in a majority, but in a sizeable minority of fishes (plaice, dab, grey gurnard, starry ray, starry smooth-hound) it is constant to within 5-10% across a 3-fold length range.

Thompson's specific plaice observation (k rising to a maximum near 30 cm and then declining) is not reproduced: in 54,375 North Sea plaice k is lowest at 5-10 cm (0.90) and at 20-25 cm (0.91) and rises monotonically to 1.01 at 45-50 cm, with no decline at large sizes; the overall exponent is 3.02 and k varies by only 5% between 13.5 and 40.5 cm. His 1909 data were from one locality and season; the pooled survey sample mixes seasons (Q1 spawning condition is about 10% lower than Q3, see claim ch03-18) and areas, which could flatten or shift a peak. Within-quarter fits were still 'variable k' in 21 of 30 species-quarter combinations.

A varying k is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, a change of form: condition, gut fullness, gonad state and ontogenetic changes in density or fat content also change W at fixed L (assessors' caveat). The test therefore addresses Thompson's empirical expectation that k will be found to vary, not his inference about form.

Lengths are 1-cm (or coarser) classes, weights are from survey scales at sea (whole-gram or coarser), sexes and years are pooled, and fish are treated as independent; the F-test P-values are therefore nominal. The 10% k-range threshold, not the P-value, is what separates taxa here.

Eutrigla appears twice (species-level and genus-level records); neither set has variable k (the genus-level set is the only taxon in which the cube law is not even rejected), so merging them would give 14/19 = 0.74.
